note: Approved cases only. Drafts are reviewed in the private Claude version before they are added here.

opts.t: Start IV ceftriaxone for a urinary tract infection.
opts.w: She has no fever, no instability and no genitourinary signs. Bacteriuria is common in older residents of care facilities, and treating it does not improve delirium. Antibiotics here add C. difficile, resistance and drug-reaction risk.

opts.t: Hold antibiotics. Look for other causes of delirium and observe closely.
opts.w: Correct. Dehydration (Na 149) and a new anticholinergic (oxybutynin) are likely contributors. Reassess promptly if fever, hemodynamic instability or urinary symptoms appear.

opts.t: Start oral nitrofurantoin as a gentler option.
opts.w: A narrower drug is still treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria. The question is whether to treat at all, not which agent.

opts.t: Treat, then repeat the urine culture to confirm clearance.
opts.w: Test-of-cure cultures are not indicated, and this treatment course isn't either. Repeat cultures tend to generate more unnecessary treatment.

cases.pearl: Bacteriuria plus confusion is not a UTI. In older patients with delirium but no genitourinary symptoms or systemic signs, IDSA recommends assessing other causes and observing rather than treating. Nurses can help most upstream: don't send urine cultures without symptoms.
cases.question: The urine culture is positive. What is the best next step?
cases.story: Brought in for two days of new confusion. Baseline mild dementia; usually conversant. Staff noted she was drinking less. She cannot reliably report urinary symptoms. No flank pain on exam. A urine sample was sent on arrival.
cases.where: Admitted from long-term care · Medicine ward · Day 0

ev: MRSA nasal PCR and de-escalation study
STOP-Vanc randomized trial, Clin Infect Dis 2026

opts.t: Continue all three antibiotics until day 7.
opts.w: The MRSA nasal PCR is negative, and he has no MRSA risk factors. Continuing vancomycin adds kidney risk; his creatinine is already rising. A fixed 7 days ignores how quickly he stabilized.

opts.t: Stop vancomycin. Continue ceftriaxone and azithromycin, switch to oral when ready, and aim for a 5-day total if he stays stable.
opts.w: Correct. A negative MRSA nasal PCR has a negative predictive value above 95% for MRSA pneumonia. ATS/IDSA guidance supports a minimum of 5 days, guided by clinical stability.

opts.t: Escalate to piperacillin-tazobactam to be safe.
opts.w: He is improving. Escalating without a sign of failure or a resistant organism adds spectrum without benefit.

opts.t: Keep vancomycin until the final sputum culture is reported.
opts.w: Waiting for a final culture delays an available de-escalation decision. The nasal PCR answers the MRSA question now.

cases.pearl: A negative test only helps if someone acts on it. In a 2026 ICU trial, the MRSA nasal PCR had a negative predictive value of 98.9%, yet vancomycin use didn't fall. The test needs a time-out that turns the result into a stop order. Pharmacists and nurses can prompt it.
cases.question: What is the best action at this review?
cases.story: Admitted with community-acquired pneumonia, right lower lobe infiltrate. In the ED he received ceftriaxone, azithromycin and vancomycin. No recent hospitalization, IV antibiotics or prior MRSA. He is now eating and walking the hallway.

ev: IDSA skin and soft tissue infection guideline, 2014
meds: Cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 h · day 3

opts.t: Continue IV cefazolin until the redness is completely gone.
opts.w: Residual erythema often takes days to fade after the infection is controlled; it isn't treatment failure. Prolonging IV therapy adds line risk and hospital days.

opts.t: Switch to oral cephalexin and stop after 5 days total. Extend only if he hasn't improved.
opts.w: Correct. IDSA recommends 5 days for uncomplicated cellulitis, extended only when the infection hasn't improved. He meets the criteria for switching from IV to oral.

opts.t: Discharge on a 14-day oral course to be safe.
opts.w: A longer course doesn't reduce relapse in uncomplicated cellulitis. Each extra day of antibiotics raises the risk of side effects and C. difficile.

opts.t: Add doxycycline for MRSA coverage before discharge.
opts.w: He is responding to a beta-lactam, with no pus, abscess or MRSA risk. Adding MRSA coverage treats a pathogen that isn't there.

cases.pearl: The shortest effective course is a safety measure, not a cost cut. Nurses can trigger the day 2–3 time-out: note when the patient is afebrile and eating, and ask whether the drug can be switched to oral and when it will stop. Every antibiotic order should have a stop date.
cases.question: What is the best plan for the rest of his course?
cases.story: Admitted with nonpurulent cellulitis of the right forearm. On IV cefazolin since admission. The marked border has receded about 60%, and pain is much better. Some pink discoloration remains. He is eating well and asking about going home.
cases.where: Medicine ward · Hospital day 3, IV cefazolin

ev: CDC: Removing inaccurate antibiotic allergy labels
meds: Allergy history: itchy rash on the trunk at age 6 while on amoxicillin for an ear infection
No hives, swelling, breathing difficulty or blistering
No penicillin since; no allergist evaluation

opts.t: Avoid all beta-lactams and give IV vancomycin.
opts.w: Nonpurulent cellulitis is mostly streptococcal, and a beta-lactam is the better drug. Vancomycin adds nephrotoxicity, monitoring and resistance pressure, all based on an unverified label.

opts.t: Record it as a low-risk history. Give cefazolin, and arrange a supervised oral amoxicillin challenge to remove the label.
opts.w: Correct. A remote, benign rash is low risk. Cefazolin has a side chain unlike amoxicillin and can be used. Low-risk labels can be tested with a direct oral challenge, often without skin testing.

opts.t: Hold antibiotics until penicillin skin testing is done.
opts.w: Delaying treatment of a febrile infection isn't justified. Skin testing isn't required for a low-risk history, and it shouldn't hold up appropriate therapy.
Clindamycin carries one of the highest C. difficile risks of any antibiotic, and streptococcal resistance to it is rising. It's a poor substitute when a beta-lactam can be used.

cases.pearl: About 10% of people in the U.S. report a penicillin allergy, but fewer than 1% of the population is truly allergic. A careful history, often taken by the nurse, is the first stewardship intervention. It opens the way to narrower, more effective drugs.
cases.question: What does this allergy history support?
cases.story: Three days of a spreading, tender, warm red area on the left lower leg, no pus or abscess. Her chart says “PENICILLIN ALLERGY.” The team is about to order IV vancomycin. During admission, the nurse takes a detailed allergy history.
